proposals.impact: reduce intro-to-q1 drop-off from 40% to under 20%
proposals.observation: Of 7 quiz sessions in the 48-hour window, 2 stalled at intro_load and 2 more stalled at q1_shown, meaning 4 out of 7 people who landed on the quiz never moved past the very first screen. Only 1 person completed it. The intro screen is the single largest drop-off point in the funnel, not the questions themselves. All 4 top-of-funnel sources (IG dominant at 4 sessions) are sending warm traffic that bounces before the quiz even begins.
proposals.proposal: The intro screen is losing people before they invest a single answer. The most common cause in short quizzes is an opening paragraph that explains the quiz rather than creating the felt sense that this is already about them. Joel's intro almost certainly opens with a description of what the quiz does. Replace that with a single, specific, scene-setting sentence that names the reader's internal experience before asking anything of them. Then reduce the CTA copy from something generic like "Start the quiz" to a phrase that continues the emotional logic of that sentence. This is a one-field edit to the intro copy block plus the button label.

proposals.impact: lift 55% open rate further and model subject-line pattern for lower-performing sequences
proposals.observation: Money Vigilance has the highest open rate of the three active automations at 55.56%, beating Money Avoidance (47%) and Money Worship (37.5%) by a meaningful margin. The sequence name and likely subject line are doing something right for this archetype. The gap between Vigilance and Worship is 18 percentage points, which is large enough to suggest a subject-line or first-line framing difference rather than list-quality variation. Studying what the Vigilance sequence is doing and applying that logic to the Worship sequence's first email subject is the lowest-effort, highest-yield email action in the window.
proposals.proposal: Pull the subject line from Money Vigilance email 1 and compare it to Money Worship email 1. The Vigilance subject almost certainly names a specific internal state or tension rather than a benefit or a type label. Rewrite the Money Worship email 1 subject to follow the same logic: name the thing the reader privately feels rather than describing what they are or what they'll get. The first-line preview text (preheader) should continue that thought rather than repeat it. This is a subject + preheader field edit in one file.

proposals.impact: convert warm blog readers into quiz starts
proposals.observation: The blog post published today, "Why is buying something I can clearly afford triggering this much guilt and remorse?", maps directly onto the Money Avoidance archetype, which has the second-highest send volume (17 emails) of the three active sequences. A reader who finds this post via search or IG and reads to the end is already inside the exact emotional territory the quiz diagnoses. There is no evidence of a quiz CTA inside the post body (no such component appears in the recent commits or content config). Adding one contextual sentence with a link at the natural close of the post's argument converts warm, self-selected readers into quiz starts without any paid spend.
proposals.proposal: Add a single closing paragraph to the guilt-and-remorse blog post that names what the reader has just done (sat with a question most people avoid) and offers the quiz as the next honest step. The paragraph must pass the Sultanic test: no other coach can write it, because it references the specific post topic and Joel's known framing. No button component needed, a plain hyperlinked sentence works and stays within a single content file edit.
proposals.new_text: If you read this far, you already know this feeling has a shape. The quiz takes four minutes and identifies which pattern is running underneath the guilt — not to label you, but because the pattern underneath is where the actual work starts. [Find your pattern here →](/quiz)
